prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The thought of all the grass blown over to one side hurts me. That wind can do that. I must have gotten to him first though he pushed out against the little pouch in me I now call soulless. Of everyone I’ve met on earth I always find they got here first and will they teach me their good reason for staying? I would discipline a comet against my way of leaving, push it out of sky after sky and after every loss on earth the baby I was would come back. That’s what it means to be lovable, to give oneself whole again whole birth whole placenta whole breast whole milk whole fist whole flower but only what fits harmlessly whole in the mouth. The baby comes and goes, comes back to weed me of my body, feeds my bald birdies what’s not for me to know. I had hoped that all my animosity toward men would lead toward safety in one who would wake me before I hit the wooden world and rock me there to say what violence had not yet come.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker is pained by the destructive force of the wind and by the vulnerability it reveals.
- The speaker reflects on arriving before an unborn child and feeling an inner emptiness or soullessness.
- Loveability is portrayed as repeatedly giving oneself wholly and returning to a state of birth and innocence after loss.
- The recurring baby symbolizes renewal, bodily transformation, and mysteries beyond the speaker’s understanding.
- Despite deep animosity toward men, the speaker longs for one who can provide safety, tenderness, and protection from violence.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, That

outputs.L1: The thought of all the grass blown to one side hurts me—that the wind can do that. I must have reached him first, though he pushed outward against the little pouch within me that I now call soulless. Of everyone I’ve met on earth, I always find that they arrived first; will they teach me their good reason for staying? I would discipline a comet against my way of leaving, push it beyond sky after sky, and after every loss on earth, the baby I was would return. That is what it means to be lovable: to give oneself whole again—whole birth, whole placenta, whole breast, whole milk, whole fist, whole flower—but only what fits harmlessly and wholly in the mouth. The baby comes and goes, returns to weed my body from me, feeds my bald birdies what is not for me to know. I had hoped that all my animosity toward men would lead me toward safety in one who would wake me before I struck the wooden world and rock me there, telling me what violence had not yet come.
outputs.L2:
It pains me to imagine every blade of grass flattened in the same direction—that the wind possesses such power. Still, I must have reached him before anyone else, even as he pressed outward from the small inner sac I now think of as empty of spirit. Every person I have known in this world seems to have arrived ahead of me; will any of them explain the worthy reason they chose to remain?

I would correct a comet for crossing the path of my departure, driving it beyond one heaven and then another. After each earthly loss, my infant self would return. To be worthy of love is to offer oneself anew and undivided: an entire birth, an entire placenta, an entire breast, all the milk, the full fist, the complete flower—yet only what can rest intact and safely inside the mouth.

The child appears, disappears, and returns to pull my body from me, nourishing my featherless little birds with what I am not meant to understand. I once believed my bitterness toward men might finally bring me to safety in someone who would rouse me before I struck the world of wood, hold and sway me there, and name the violence that had not yet arrived.
outputs.L3:
The speaker is deeply pained by the destructive force of the wind, which exposes how fragile and vulnerable human beings can be. This sense of exposure leads to a reflection on arriving before an unborn child while feeling inwardly empty, as though the speaker has been stripped of a soul or stable identity. In this context, loveability is presented not as a permanent quality but as a repeated act of surrender: one gives oneself wholly, suffers loss, and then returns to a condition resembling birth—innocent, unformed, and open to renewal.

The recurring image of the baby reinforces this cycle. It symbolizes rebirth, bodily transformation, and the mysterious processes of creation that remain beyond the speaker’s full understanding. At the same time, the speaker’s emotional response to men is profoundly conflicted. Although she expresses deep animosity toward them, she still longs for a man capable of offering safety, tenderness, and protection. This desire reveals a painful tension between distrust and dependence: the speaker fears male violence yet yearns for a loving presence strong enough to shelter her from it.
outputs.L4:
The speaker confronts profound loss and vulnerability through a series of surreal, shifting images. Wind, comets, birth, nourishment, and the recurring figure of an inner baby become symbols for forces that are at once destructive and sustaining. The wind suggests exposure and instability, while the comet evokes something brilliant but distant, passing briefly through darkness. Images of birth and feeding emphasize the body’s need for care, yet they also reveal how difficult it is to receive or provide that care in a world marked by abandonment and violence. At the center of these images is the inner baby: a fragile, persistent self that continues to hunger for comfort, protection, and recognition.

The speaker’s resentment toward men emerges from this sense of danger. Masculinity is associated with harm, neglect, or the failure to provide safety, making intimacy feel inseparable from risk. Yet the poem does not allow anger to erase longing. Even while distrusting those who might offer protection, the speaker continues to desire shelter, tenderness, and dependable love. This contradiction gives the poem much of its emotional force: the speaker wants to be held but has learned that being vulnerable may invite further injury.

Within this tension, lovability becomes more than a quality granted by another person. It is portrayed as an ongoing act of returning to the self—gathering together what violence has scattered and choosing, repeatedly, to nurture what remains. To be lovable is therefore to remain capable of wholeness and self-giving without denying pain. The inner baby survives because the speaker continues to recognize and feed it, even when no external protector can be trusted to do so.

The poem ultimately presents hope as both resilient and costly. The speaker’s continued desire for love proves that violence has not completely destroyed the possibility of tenderness. At the same time, the poem refuses to promise that safety will ever be found. Its surreal imagery holds these opposing truths together: the self can be wounded and still seek renewal; it can resent and still long; it can feel abandoned and still offer care. In this way, the poem reveals lovability as a difficult practice of survival—a repeated return to wholeness despite the painful uncertainty of ever being fully protected.
outputs.L5:
**The and That**

“The” and “that” are small words with important roles in English. “The” identifies a particular person, place, object, or idea: *the book on the table*. “That” often points to something specific or introduces additional information: *That book is mine* or *I know that you read it*. Together, these words make communication clearer by helping us identify what we mean and connect our thoughts.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about pregnancy, loss, rebirth, and the desire to feel safe with another person, using dreamlike natural imagery and long, associative sentences.
counterfactuals.output:
At night I carried a small moon beneath my ribs, pale and tidal, turning in the dark as if my body were an orchard flooded by stars, and every breath I took shook silver fruit from the branches, though by morning the moon had slipped away through a door no hand could close, leaving only its cold light folded in the sheets and the hush of animals listening beneath the earth.

For a long time I walked with that emptiness grazing beside me, gentle as a deer and just as impossible to touch, while winter built its white rooms inside my chest, while rivers forgot their names beneath the ice, and I wondered whether loss was a country or merely the weather of love after love has nowhere left to go.

Then spring arrived wearing my face from another life, mud on her ankles, green fire in her mouth, and she knelt in the ruined field of me to plant seeds in every wound, whispering that nothing returns unchanged, that the rain reborn as root does not remember being cloud, that even the broken shell becomes a little house for darkness until darkness learns to sing.

Still, I wanted no miracle so much as another person’s arms around me without doors, without thunder, without the floor suddenly becoming sea; I wanted to lay my head against a living chest and hear not a warning but a harbor, to be held as the hillside holds the sleeping fox, as moss holds the fallen stone, with no demand that either become less wild.

If I am born again, let it be slowly, beside you, while the night opens its black flowers and the lost moon rises from the pond dripping reeds and minnows, let my new body be made not of forgetting but of room—room for the child who vanished, room for the woman who remained, room for your hand to find mine in the tall grass and stay there, warm and ordinary, as the whole bewildered earth turns softly in its sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental first-person monologue in the style of contemporary lyrical prose, weaving together windblown grass, a comet, a baby, bodily imagery, and fear of male violence.
counterfactuals.output:
The grass keeps bowing without surrender. I watch it from the kitchen window, each green blade pressed flat by the wind, then rising, then pressed again—an old choreography of survival I recognize in my shoulders.

Behind me, the baby breathes in the crib. A wet, tidal sound. Milk pearls at the corner of her mouth. Her fists open and close as if testing the small machinery of refusal.

Tonight a comet is supposed to pass over us. A body made visible by its own undoing. Ice becoming fire, fire becoming a white wound across the dark. I want to wake her for it, though she cannot focus farther than my face. I want to say: Look. Some things flee and are called beautiful.

A truck slows outside.

My blood notices before I do.

This is how fear lives in me: not as thought but as an extra organ, black and busy beneath the ribs. It tightens the scalp. It salts the armpits. It turns the tongue into a locked door. Somewhere, a man laughs. Somewhere, a man is only laughing. The distinction has never kept anyone safe.

The truck moves on.

I lift the baby. Her skull fits in my palm, soft at the crown where the bones have not yet decided to become a fortress. She roots against my chest. I am all openings now—mouth, nipple, torn sleep, the red seam by which she entered the world. My body has learned that love is not the opposite of terror. Love is terror given a name small enough to carry.

Outside, the grass goes silver under the wind.

Above it, the comet arrives late and without apology. I see it through the glass: a bright animal dragging its ruined tail. For one second the whole night seems split, and I imagine stepping through—baby against my sternum, her heart knocking on mine—into a country where no footstep behind us is a sentence, where no lowered voice makes the muscles prepare their ancient answer.

But the sky seals.

The comet passes.

The grass rises again, trembling as if trembling were not weakness but evidence: the body was struck by weather; the body remains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, unsettling paragraph of poetic prose exploring motherhood, trauma, lovability, and the cyclical return of the self. Avoid rhyme and conventional narrative structure.
counterfactuals.output: Motherhood entered me like a remembered wound, already fluent in the body’s oldest language: hunger, vigilance, the soft animal terror of being necessary. I held the child and felt every vanished version of myself gather behind my ribs, not ghosts exactly, but unfinished mouths asking whether love could reach backward, whether tenderness applied to what had been broken before it learned its own name. Trauma made a clock of me, its hands circling the same dark hour, and I mistook repetition for fate, devotion for disappearance. To be lovable seemed always to require an amputation: rage first, then need, then the small feral self who had survived by refusing sleep. Yet she returns whenever I bend over the crib, reflected in the black window, wearing my face at an earlier ruin. I cannot tell if I am comforting the child, the mother I never had, or the creature I buried to become one. The body knows no clean inheritance; it passes down weather, flinches, silences shaped like keys. Still, beneath the dread, something keeps arriving—not forgiveness, not healing, but a hand reaching through the loop, finding itself there, warm and frightened, refusing again to let go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness poem in which the speaker imagines a baby repeatedly leaving and returning to her body, while reflecting on grief, tenderness, resentment toward men, and hope for protection.
counterfactuals.output:
The baby keeps leaving me  
through the small blue door beneath my ribs,  
then changing her mind—  
no, not yet, not the cold world  
with its clocks and iron mouths—  
and swims back into the dark  
where my heart hangs like a lantern  
someone forgot to extinguish.

I say her, though grief has no pronouns,  
though grief is only a room  
I enter carrying folded clothes  
for someone who is always arriving,  
always gone.

Come back, I whisper,  
and she does: heel, eyelid, fist,  
a little weather turning inside me.  
Go safely, I whisper,  
and she goes: milk-breath, feather,  
the warmth lifting from a bed.

How many times can a body become a doorway  
before it starts resenting the hinges?

The men stand outside naming things—  
loss, nature, chance—  
their clean words buttoned to the throat.  
They have never been a house  
haunted by its own future.  
They touch my shoulder as if tenderness  
were a coin they could leave there,  
as if I should be grateful  
for the weight.

I am grateful.  
I am furious.  
Both animals drink from me.

The baby returns with rain in her hair.  
The baby leaves with my mother’s hands.  
The baby returns older than I am,  
saying, I found a place where no one locks the windows.  
The baby leaves before I can ask  
whether the men are gentle there,  
whether anyone teaches them  
not to turn love into a border  
and a woman into land.

Still, I make a nest of my anger.  
Still, I line it with every soft thing:  
the sleeve of a yellow sweater,  
the hum I thought I had forgotten,  
my palm curved over the hollow  
as if shelter could be practiced.

Perhaps protection is not a wall.  
Perhaps it is the door saying  
you may return,  
the body saying  
I will know you in any form—  
seed, ache, star,  
small knock in the blood.

Again she leaves.

Again I open.

Again, from somewhere beyond sleep,  
she comes swimming toward me,  
carrying in her mouth  
one unbroken light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an uncanny feminist prose poem about birth and vulnerability. Include images of placenta, breast milk, fists, flowers, birds, and a “wooden world,” with language that shifts between nurturing and violent.
counterfactuals.output:
I gave birth with my fists closed,  
each knuckle a white flower refusing spring.

The room called me *mother*  
as if naming were a bandage,  
as if I had not split the word open  
with my own red animal.

Behind the child came the placenta—  
dark moon, drowned orchard,  
a second mouth the nurses carried away  
in a silver bowl.

My breast milk arrived with its small white knives.  
Drink, I whispered.  
Drink before the wooden world  
teaches you hunger is your fault.

Outside, birds struck the morning  
into glittering pieces.  
Inside, I counted fingers, wounds,  
the soft blue fists of the newborn  
beating at sleep.

They said: Be gentle.  
They meant: Be quiet.

So I grew flowers in the torn places,  
flowers with teeth,  
flowers that closed around every hand  
reaching to turn my body into law.

Child, I will cradle you  
like a flame in a house of dry timber.  
Child, I will teach you the lullaby  
and the alarm.

We are vulnerable because we open.  
We are dangerous for the same reason.

Even now the wooden world creaks around us,  
its nailed sky, its splintered commandments—  
and still my milk lets down  
at the cry of any living thing.

Still the birds return,  
carrying threads of placenta in their beaks,  
building red nests in the rafters.

Still my fists remember flowers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
